question: The increasing provision of specialised and complex medical procedures in private outpatient healthcare units raises important questions regarding the suitability and licensing of facilities, compliance with health standards and the professional qualifications, specialised education and continuous training of healthcare professionals.

Ensuring that these procedures are carried out by adequately trained personnel, in appropriately licensed and equipped facilities, is a key prerequisite for the quality of services and patient protection.

In the context of the free movement of professionals, mutual recognition of professional qualifications and lifelong learning, it is important to examine the extent to which the European framework responds to new requirements for specialisation and developments in the healthcare sector. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider that the current European framework is sufficient to ensure that complex medical procedures are performed in appropriately licensed and equipped facilities by healthcare professionals with the requisite qualifications, specialised training and clinical experience?

Does the Commission intend to examine, alongside Member States, the need to strengthen European guidelines and exchange of best practices on the supervision of private healthcare providers, the licensing of specialised medical procedures and the continuing professional training of healthcare professionals?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.11.2026) In line with Articles 165 and 168 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the EU supports and complements the actions of the Member States in the field of education and public health.

In this regard, EU actions must respect the competences of the Member States for the definition of their health policy and for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care. Consequently, EU law does not provide a framework for the management of health care. It does not regulate how, where and when complex medical procedures should be performed, or who should be licensed to perform them.

That said, the Commission encourages reform efforts through the European Semester and provides funding to improve access to quality healthcare, for example by devising measures addressing quality assurance, accreditation, patient safety, outcome measurement and performance assessment.

Directive 2005/36/EC1 supports the free movement of professionals by setting out procedural rules for cross-border recognition of professional qualifications obtained in the EU. Several healthcare professions, including doctors, are covered by the ‘automatic’ recognition system, based on EU-wide minimum training requirements.

The Commission monitors scientific and technical progress and changes in national legislations and uses its delegated powers to update the minimum training requirements, with the aim to support patient safety and to reflect current healthcare standards in the Member States. However, the Directive itself is not a standard-setting instrument.
It does not impose conditions for authorisation to open a private practice, either, leaving this matter to the Member States, in line with their competences.
